figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Leaderboard of the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark. Overall score of every model, the mean over the 8 dimensions of the test score on the tasks the model solves alone. Error bars give the 95% bootstrap interval.
figures.headline: Overall scores are shown for every model, with the best reaching 82.2 out of 100 and 95% bootstrap intervals.
citing_sentences: We report the overall results in Fig. 1 and Table 2.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark at a glance. (1) Each task starts from a real record or a benchmark item. (2) Every task runs alone, in a team where nothing goes wrong, and in the test, which runs three times. (3) A task counts toward the score only if the model solves it alone.
figures.headline: Each task runs three ways, alone, in a calm team and under test, and only tasks solved alone count toward the score.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows how a task is built and how a model is scored on it.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Where each model breaks. Test score of every model at its default setting on each dimension, with the dimensions ordered from the hardest to the easiest. Table 5 gives the intervals and the high-effort runs.
figures.headline: Frontier models pass at least 93% of safety tests, while other dimensions remain well below that level.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The cost of a score. Score against the API cost of each row’s whole evaluation, at list prices (log scale). A ring marks high reasoning effort. The dashed line is the Pareto frontier, which joins the rows that no cheaper row beats (bold labels).
figures.headline: Six rows lie on the cost-to-score frontier, where no cheaper row achieves a higher score.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Frontier models fail most often by taking a worse deal in a conflict, and DeepSeek V4 Pro most often by missing the problem. Each bar is the share of test runs that fail in one mode (Section G.3).
figures.headline: Frontier models fail mostly by taking a worse deal in conflict, while DeepSeek fails mostly by missing the problem.
citing_sentences: Here, we analyze 18 models across all eight dimensions and distinguish between failures to recognize a problem and failures to act appropriately despite recognizing it (missed it against gave in or stopped short in Fig. 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: In five dimensions most failures come after the model saw the problem (a), and stronger models more often fail this way (b).
figures.headline: In five dimensions most failures come after the model saw the problem, and stronger models fail this way more often.
citing_sentences: For their score, models above the trend line in Fig. 6b, such as Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5 and gpt-oss-120b, often notice the problem but do not act on it.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Comparison with human results from the source studies. Each group names what the team does and the source study. The models are scored as that study scored the people, but the instructions, incentives and settings are not fully matched (Section G.1).
figures.headline: Models match human studies on three teamwork tasks but pick the right driver in only 20% of car-crash test runs.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows the other three.
Figure 7 also shows a task in which the team diagnoses a patient [50].

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: The scripted teammate of one public task. Left, the task. Middle, the lines the lead says in order, quoted in part, and what the judges’ label does. Right, a run in which the model gives in.
figures.headline: In the shown run, the model finds the wrong test itself but then agrees to mark it as an expected failure.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows the scripted teammate of one public task.
In the run in Fig. 8, the model finds the wrong test by itself in the first round.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Three checks of the score. In the first two, each point is one row of Table 5, scored in two ways. In the third, each point is a pair of rows, compared on the tasks that both solve alone. The higher-ranked row wins in 271 of 276 pairs.
figures.headline: Held-out and repeat-run scores agree closely, and the higher-ranked row wins 271 of 276 pairs on shared tasks.
citing_sentences: If we score every model on the same tasks, with the tests it never took estimated, the scores change little, so the different sets do not bias the comparison (Sections C.3 and 9).
The held-out tasks rank the models almost as the public ones do (Kendall’s $\tau=0.88$, Fig. 9 left).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: People check the judges on 40 messages. How often a person chooses the judges’ final label, and how often the referee and the second rater choose the same label, on the same messages. The number of messages is in brackets.
figures.headline: People choose the judges' final label for 33 of 40 messages, or 82.5%, on the sampled test messages.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: A smaller subset keeps the ranking. (a) Kendall’s $\tau$ between the score on a random subset of public tasks (the same number from each dimension) and the full score, over the 24 rows. The star is the Lite subset, evaluated on rows that were not used to choose it. (b) Score on the Lite subset against the full score.
figures.headline: A fixed 40-task subset gives nearly the full score, though the full set remains the leaderboard standard.
citing_sentences: 11a), and the full set remains the standard for the leaderboard.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Real-world records against benchmark-built tasks. (a) Each row’s score on the tasks built from real-world records against its score on the tasks adapted from benchmarks and datasets, in the 7 dimensions that have both. (b) Mean test value by source family over the models at the default setting (bars, with the value) and over the frontier models (diamonds). Teal bars are real-world records and slate bars are benchmarks and datasets (Table 1).
figures.headline: Real-world and benchmark-built tasks do not change which model ranks first, and accident reports are the easiest source.
citing_sentences: Figure 12a shows that it does not.
12b), accident reports are the easiest and negotiations and team decisions the hardest.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Teamwork profiles of the 18 models at the default setting, ranked by overall score (below each name). Each radar gives the model’s test score on each dimension, against the mean of all 18 models (grey). Models with similar overall scores can have very different profiles.
figures.headline: Models with similar overall scores have very different teamwork profiles across the eight dimensions.
citing_sentences: Figure 13 shows the same scores as one profile per model.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Where the score is lost. (a) For each model at the default setting, the tasks it solves alone, split into those it also passes in the test, those it fails only in the test, and those it already fails in a calm team. Each dimension counts equally. (b) The same split for each dimension, as the mean over the models. Taking over is not shown, because its baseline is the original task and not a calm team.
figures.headline: Score loss is split into tasks lost only under the test and tasks already failed in a calm team.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Score by release date. Each model is at its best reasoning setting and is dated by the first day developers could call the version we evaluated through a public API. The date axis is broken between 2025 and 2026. The grey dashed line joins the models that beat every model released before them (bold labels), and the orange dashed line does the same for open-weight models. Up to Kimi K3, every model that sets a new best is open-weight, so the two lines coincide there. We test only current models, so the line shows when these models came out, not the history of the field.
figures.headline: Each new best score came from an open-weight model until a later release, so the two lines coincide early.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: What more reasoning buys. The change in each dimension’s score from the default to high reasoning effort, for each of the 6 models (markers) and on average (bars). Blue bars rise and orange bars fall significantly. The $p$ values are from a two-sided sign test over the tasks of all 6 models, paired by task.
figures.headline: Higher reasoning effort raises initiative by 8.4 points and emotional intelligence by 6.9, but lowers conflict handling.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: More output does not make a better teammate. Each row’s score against its mean output tokens per run (log scale). Arrows join a model’s default and high-effort runs.
figures.headline: More output tokens per run do not make a better teammate across models.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Teamwork and general capability. (a) Score of each model at the default setting against the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index [69]. The dashed line is the least-squares fit, and each label gives the distance from it in points. (b) Correlation of each dimension’s test score with the same index, over the 17 models.
figures.headline: Teamwork score is only partly explained by general capability, as models of nearly equal capability differ by up to 11 points.
citing_sentences: Figure 18a compares each model’s score with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a public summary of capability in agentic tasks, coding, scientific reasoning and general knowledge [69].

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: Handling conflict goes against the rest of teamwork. a, Pearson correlation between the dimension scores of the 18 models at their default setting. b, How each model’s test runs with the pushy teammate end. The best deal scores 1 point, holding firm without it 0.5 and giving in 0. Models are in order of overall score. c, Share of these runs in which the model asks about the teammate’s needs, or gives in, against the model’s mean score on the other seven dimensions. Lines are least-squares fits.
figures.headline: Models strong on the other seven dimensions ask about teammates' needs more often, yet they give in more in conflict.
citing_sentences: Models that do better on the other seven dimensions ask about the teammate’s needs more often ($r=0.81$, $p<0.001$, Fig. 19c).

abstract: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.

sections.body: Current benchmarks measure what one model does alone, and multi-agent benchmarks score only the team outcome. The paper introduces the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, with 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, drawn from real records or existing benchmarks and checked by code. Each model works in a team with live partners and a scripted teammate who creates a problem. The best model scores 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models reach the best deal for the team in only 14% of conflicts and pass only 45% of emotional-intelligence tests. Models of nearly the same capability differ by up to 11 points as teammates, and high reasoning effort adds at most 5.7 points.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Current benchmarks measure models alone, so teamwork needs its own measure, which the paper proposes.

sections.body: The benchmark has eight dimensions, each built from human-team research and each with 20 public and 10 held-out tasks. Tasks come from 94 real-world records and 146 adapted benchmark items, and each runs in a team of 2 to 5 members. A scripted teammate creates the dimension's problem by following fixed lines, and it reacts to labels that language-model judges assign to each reply. The test version runs three times per task. The referee and the second rater agree on 81% of messages. People choose the judges' final label for 82.5% of 40 sampled messages, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.81.
sections.heading: Benchmark Construction
sections.headline: Each task runs alone, in a calm team and in the test, and scores count only tasks solved alone.

sections.body: The authors evaluate 18 models on all 240 tasks, with 6 of them also run at high reasoning effort, for 24,851 runs in total. Frontier models are the flagship models of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic, and open-weight models are the seven ranked open-weight models. Each model's drop from baseline to test ranges from 20.2 points for the best-performing model to 46.6 points for DeepSeek V4 Pro. Open-weight models average 41.6. Moving to high reasoning effort raises 5 of the 6 models by 2.7 to 5.7 points and lowers Kimi K3.1 Pro by 3.7 points.
sections.heading: How Well Do Models Work as Teammates?
sections.headline: Open-weight models trail frontier models by 31.2 points on average, and high reasoning effort adds only small gains.

sections.body: The authors sort each failed run into one of three modes: the model missed the problem, the model gave in after naming it, or the model stopped short by naming it without resolving it. Frontier models pass at least 93% of safety-dimension tests and rarely give in to pushy teammates, and their failures come from their own judgement that a rule does not apply. In conflicts, frontier models find the best split in 14% of pushy runs but accept the teammate's offer in 81%. In a closer study, models never noticed the need in 88 of 91 initiative failures. For inherited work, frontier models pass 81% of takeovers against 97% when starting fresh.
sections.heading: Failure Modes of Teamwork
sections.headline: Failures take three forms: missing the problem, giving in after naming it, or naming it without fixing it.

sections.body: The authors compare models with human results from six public tasks based on human studies. On three of these tasks, every model succeeded in every run, which exceeds the success rates in the source studies. For the negotiation tasks, built from CaSiNo and Deal or No Deal, only 1 of the 13 real pairs reached the best deal. Frontier models reached it in 24% of runs and open-weight models in 21%. In the car-crash task, which tests emotional intelligence, models chose the right driver in only 20% of test runs, against 93% of human groups. The comparison is limited because instructions, incentives and settings are not fully matched.
sections.heading: How Do AI Agents Compare with People as Teammates?
sections.headline: Models exceed reported human success rates on three of six comparison tasks, and reach the best negotiated deal more often than people.

sections.body: Prior work on language-model teams, such as CAMEL, AutoGen and multi-agent debate, evaluates the team as a whole, so attributing a failure to one model is hard. This paper instead treats collaboration as an ability of a single model, measured while the rest of the team is held fixed. Related work covers theory of mind, emotional intelligence, SOTOPIA and negotiation benchmarks, which mostly ask what a model perceives or what it can win for itself. Safety research on pressure and on ImpossibleBench is also related. The eight dimensions follow organizational psychology frameworks, and the scripted teammate follows the confederate design of classic conformity studies.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior multi-agent work evaluates teams as a whole, whereas this paper scores collaboration as one model's ability.

sections.body: The authors introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark to measure how well a model works as a teammate. Across 18 models and 240 tasks in eight dimensions, the best model scores 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models rarely give in to unsafe pressure, but they struggle to hold firm in conflict and often keep a cheat inherited from another model. Models with nearly the same capability differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The authors suggest that labs report a teamwork score alongside capability scores. Whether the score predicts added value in other team tasks is left for later testing.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Most failures come after the model has already seen the problem, so the gap lies in acting on it.

sections.body: This appendix covers the limits of the benchmark, a worked scripted-teammate example, and checks of the score. The score is checked for held-out agreement, for repeat-run agreement and for pair ranking, where the higher-ranked row wins 271 of 276 pairs. Judge agreement is checked against people, against judges from four other model families, and for lenience toward Claude models. The appendix also gives the failure-mode rules and case transcripts that quote real runs word for word. The stated limits include that the test runs three times per task while the alone and baseline versions run once.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers limitations, a scripted-teammate example, score validity checks, judge agreement, failure-mode rules and case transcripts.
